Then I picked the voice back up, because I've got people to protect and I can't afford to be fourth. It isn't peace, it's just knowing.

moments.prompt: He's asked you to stand as his second in the duel.

options.text: I'll stand as your second.
options.reply: Jamme, let's go, then. Watch his feet, not his blade, and tell me afterwards what you saw.

options.text: Why does it matter whose arm it is?
options.reply: Because fourth was mine. Whatever this is, I'm not sure it's mine.

moments.prompt: After the wipe he's furious, mostly about everybody's footwork.
moments.line: Mannaggia, everyone's feet were wrong. You can't win a bout with your weight on your heels.

options.text: Show us how to stand, then.
options.reply: Weight forward, knees soft, and never cross your feet. There, you're already better.

options.text: This isn't fencing.
options.reply: Everything's fencing, uagliò. You're just losing at it.

lines.bored_warning: Uagliò, we keep fighting the same clumsy things. There's no art in it. Find me an opponent worth the effort.
lines.leaving_good: That was beautiful, all of it. I'm going back to the Monastery Grounds to watch the Scarlets drill. Come and find me.
lines.leaving_bored: I'm going back to the Monastery. This is clumsy and boring, and I'd rather watch the Scarlets make mistakes.
lines.after_wipe: Mannaggia, everybody's feet were wrong. Up, and stand properly this time.
lines.wipe_warning: We keep losing in here, and it's ugly. I'll finish this run, then I need a break.
lines.wipe_leave: I finished it, as I said. Now I'm going back to the Monastery Grounds for a while.
lines.zone_warning: We're out of our weight class here, uagliò. Pride is one thing, being stupid is another.
lines.zone_leave: I'm stopping here. We're out of our weight class. I'll be on the Scarlet Monastery Grounds.
lines.gear_refuse: No, uagliò, that's mine. A fencer doesn't give up his kit to strangers.
lines.gear_taken: Take it, then. I'm good enough without it, unfortunately for everyone else.
lines.gear_short: I'm still missing that piece. It's affecting my balance, and I notice my balance.
lines.gear_upgrade: Bellissimo, look at that. Thank you, truly.
lines.back: I'm back, and I've found three new holes in the Scarlet drills. Where are we going?
lines.send_word: Enzo has sent word from the Scarlet Monastery Grounds. He's ready to come out and show off.
lines.walkout_talk: I left angry, and I'll tell you why, honestly. Then you tell me, and we'll call it a draw.
lines.neglect: There you are! I'd started to think you'd found a better swordsman. There isn't one.
lines.asked_to_stay: Jamme, one more bout. Then I rest.
lines.on_break: Enzo is back on the Scarlet Monastery Grounds. Come back after you've done a few more jobs.

stages.stranger: My name's Esteban, and I'm a bloodmage. Before I use it on you I'll tell you what it costs and ask if you agree, every time. I'd ask you to answer honestly, and not to pretend afterwards that I didn't ask.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Valparaíso, in Chile, from one of the steep hills above the harbour where the old lifts creak up the slopes. My father worked the docks and my mother was a seamstress. I was a vascular and trauma surgeon at the city hospital for nineteen years. Car crashes, stabbings, accidents at the port. A great deal of it under X-ray, hence the badge.
stages.companion: I was scrubbed in, in the middle of an operation, when it happened. I landed in Stranglethorn in theatre clothes. I never married. My sister Paz is in the capital, or was, with her children, and I was their favourite uncle because I'd explain exactly how bones heal. I haven't found her on any list. I spent two years in the jungle before I came here to work with the healers.
stages.friend: In Stranglethorn the Bloodsail paid me to keep their injured alive. One night their captain was dying, and there was a prisoner below, dying too. I took the prisoner's blood to save the captain, and I didn't ask him. The prisoner died. I left the next morning. That's why I ask everyone now, and that's why I'm writing the clauses. There's a camp in the jungle where bloodmages are bleeding prisoners for profit. I'd like your help to stop it.
stages.sworn: The healers in Orgrimmar argued about my clauses for three days. They changed two and added one of their own, and then they adopted them for every bloodmage who wants to work here. I've taught my first class, three of them. On the first day I told them about the prisoner on the Bloodsail ship, because I want them to know why the first clause is there. It's regrettable that it took a death to write it. It won't take another.

moments.prompt: Before a fight, he asks if he may draw on your blood if things go badly.

options.text: Yes. Thank you for asking.
options.reply: Thank you for answering. You'd be surprised how few people do.

options.text: Just do whatever you need to.
options.reply: That's not an answer, I'm afraid. I'll ask again when you've thought about it.

options.text: No, not mine.
options.reply: Then I won't. I'm grateful for a clear no.

moments.prompt: He's just told you about the prisoner.

options.text: You've spent every day since making it right.
options.reply: I've spent every day since trying. That's not the same, but thank you.

options.text: You saved the captain.
options.reply: I did save him. I didn't have the right to choose which of them it would be.

lines.bored_warning: We've done the same work for some time now with nothing to show for it. I'd like to do something useful, or I'd like to go back to the healers.
lines.leaving_good: That was good work, and nobody paid a price they didn't agree to. I'm going back to Orgrimmar for a while. You know where I'll be.
lines.leaving_bored: I'm going back to Orgrimmar. We've stopped doing anything that matters out here, and there are patients there.
lines.after_wipe: Everyone stay still while I look at you. We'll discuss what went wrong when I've finished.
lines.wipe_warning: We've died in here too many times. I'll finish this run, because I don't leave a patient on the table, but afterwards I'll need a break.
lines.wipe_leave: I've seen it through, and now I'm going back to Orgrimmar. That was regrettable, all of it.
lines.zone_warning: I'd like to be precise. Everything here is beyond us, and staying is a choice to be hurt. I'd rather we didn't make it.
lines.zone_leave: I'm stopping here. I named the price of staying and you paid it anyway. I'll be in Orgrimmar.
lines.gear_refuse: I'd prefer to keep that. I don't know you well enough yet.
lines.gear_taken: Very well, I'll work without it, but please understand there'll be a cost.
lines.gear_short: I'm still missing that piece. I mention it as a clinical observation.
lines.gear_upgrade: That's well made, and very kind. Thank you.
lines.back: I'm back, and my patients are stable. Where do you need me?
lines.send_word: Esteban has sent word from Orgrimmar. His patients are stable and he's ready to come out.
lines.walkout_talk: I left in anger, which I don't approve of in myself. May I explain why? Then I'd like to hear your view, in full.
lines.neglect: It's been a while. I'd begun to wonder if I'd said something regrettable.
lines.asked_to_stay: Very well, one more, and then I've got patients waiting.
lines.on_break: Esteban is back with the healers in Orgrimmar. Come back after you've done a few more jobs.
lines.quest_abandoned: We agreed to that and left it unfinished. That's regrettable, and somebody's paying for it.

stages.stranger: I'm Fiona, and I'm a witch hunter. I'll stand in front, and I'll question everything everybody tells us, including you. Don't take it personally, it's the job.
stages.acquaintance: Aberdeen, the oil city, born and raised. My dad worked the rigs and my mum was a school secretary. I did accountancy and then nine years investigating fraud for an energy company. Padded invoices, ghost contractors, cooked safety records. I flew out to rigs in a survival suit and interviewed men who didn't want to talk to me.
stages.companion: My brother Graeme went offshore like our dad. I found a cooked safety record on his rig once, and I reported it, and they shut it for a month. Half the crew never forgave me. Graeme did, eventually. I was on a helicopter out to a rig when this happened, and I landed on a beach here with my survival whistle still clipped on. I haven't found him or my mum.
stages.friend: Here's the thing I worked out in my second year, and it's not flattering. I'd been treating this war like a casework backlog, ticking things off. People aren't entries. And my catalogue's nearly done. It points at the cult's hiding place. I need the last evidence from the jungle, and then I need somebody in authority to finally act on it. Help me do it.
stages.sworn: They acted, fast and hard, too fast. They used my catalogue as a list and raided a village I'd marked pattern consistent, unconfirmed, and innocent fishermen died alongside the cult. My work, used without the care I put into it. I burned my copy on the beach. Then I started again from page one, slower, with every unconfirmed in red, and I go to every raid myself now. Being right was never the hard part.

moments.prompt: She hands you a quest giver's story and says one detail doesn't fit.

options.text: Check it with her.
options.reply: Thank you. Nobody ever just checks. Right, here's the bit that bothers me.

options.text: It's probably nothing.
options.reply: It's usually something. I'll need that in writing if you're sure.

moments.prompt: She's asked you to help her finish the catalogue.

options.text: Let's get the last evidence.
options.reply: Aye, that's good. Facts first, conclusions after, and we write everything down.

options.text: Are you sure they'll listen this time?
options.reply: No, I'm not. That's why you're coming.

lines.bored_warning: We've done the same thing repeatedly and I've nothing new to write down. Find us something that needs investigating.
lines.leaving_good: That was useful, and I've got pages of notes. I'm going back to Booty Bay to file them. You know where I'll be.
lines.leaving_bored: I'm going back to Booty Bay. Nothing out here needs investigating, and my files do.
lines.after_wipe: Right, I'll need everybody's account of what happened. One at a time, facts first.
lines.wipe_warning: We keep dying in here and nobody's asking why. I'll finish this run, then I'm taking a break.
lines.wipe_leave: I've seen it through. Now I'm going back to Booty Bay. Come back when you've read my notes on that.
lines.zone_warning: I've assessed this place, and the evidence says we're outmatched. I'd like that noted before we go further.
lines.zone_leave: I'm stopping here. I noted that we were outmatched. I'll be in Booty Bay.
lines.gear_refuse: No, that's mine. I don't hand evidence over without a chain of custody.
lines.gear_taken: Take it, then. I've written down that you have it.
lines.gear_short: I'm still missing that piece. It's in my notes, in red.
lines.gear_upgrade: That's well made. Thank you. I'll note it.
lines.back: I'm back, and I've filed everything. Where are we going, and what do we know?
lines.send_word: Fiona has sent word from Booty Bay. Her files are in order and she's ready to come out.
lines.walkout_talk: I walked out, and I've written down why. Sit down and I'll read it to you. Then you can give me your account.
lines.neglect: You've been gone a while. I kept notes on how long, obviously.
lines.asked_to_stay: Fine, one more, but I'm taking notes.
lines.on_break: Fiona is back in Booty Bay with her files. Come back after you've done a few more jobs.
lines.quest_abandoned: We took that on and dropped it. Somebody will notice, and I'll have to write it down.

stages.stranger: I'm Freja, and I'm a midwife, or I was. Here I'm whoever's nearest when somebody's bleeding. When I tell you to do something in a fight, do it, and we'll argue about it afterwards. I like arguing afterwards.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Aarhus, in Denmark. I worked six years at the university hospital, mostly nights, and before that I played handball for twelve years on the pivot, which is where you take the most hits. My husband William is American. He fell off his bicycle outside the hospital on an icy morning and I strapped his wrist on the pavement. He asked me out before I'd finished the bandage.
stages.companion: I was finishing a night shift when it happened, and William was at work at the airport in Billund. I landed here in my hospital clothes and went straight to the infirmary and worked, because there were a lot of hurt people and work is something to hold on to. My parents were in Aarhus. I've checked the Danish lists at two hubs and none of them are on there, and William wouldn't be on a Danish list anyway. I write him a letter every week. I don't send them.
stages.friend: I'll tell you what I'm frightened of, and then we won't talk about it again. I'm frightened that one day I'll freeze at the wrong moment and somebody will die because of it. It's never happened. And I'm frightened I'll find William and he'll be different. There's a trader saying an American is fixing goblin flying machines on the Shimmering Flats and swearing at them. That sounds like my idiot. I want to go and look.
stages.sworn: He said I took my time. I hit him on the arm and then I didn't let go of him for about an hour. And I delivered a baby the same day, a goblin baby, early and in a hurry, and I didn't freeze. William's carving me a new horn. We were going to try for children the spring after all this happened. I haven't said that out loud before. We might try again.

moments.prompt: She's just told you about the American on the Shimmering Flats.

options.text: Then we're going. Today.
options.reply: Good, I was going anyway, but it's nicer with you.

options.text: It might not be him.
options.reply: I know that. I'm a midwife, I know how hope works. I'm still going.

options.text: What if he's different?
options.reply: Then I'll find out, won't I. Don't ask me that one again.

moments.prompt: After the wipe, she's on her knees checking everyone before anyone's said anything.
moments.line: Everybody stay down for a second while I look at you. Then you can tell me whose fault it was.

options.text: It was mine. I pulled too early.
options.reply: Yes, it was. Thank you for saying it. Now drink something.

options.text: We're fine, let's go again.
options.reply: You're fine when I say you're fine. Sit there until I do.

lines.bored_warning: We've killed a lot of the same thing and nobody's needed me in a while. I didn't come out here to stand at the back. Can we go and do something that matters?
lines.leaving_good: That was a good trip, and I won most of the arguments. I'm going back to the Valley to check on my women and the farms. You know where I'll be.
lines.leaving_bored: I'm going back to the Valley. There are people there who need a healer, and out here we're just hitting things for the sake of it.
lines.after_wipe: Right, nobody's dead for good. Next time we stop when I tell you to stop.
lines.wipe_warning: That's too many wipes. I'll finish this run with you because I don't leave in the middle of things, but after this I'm taking a break.
lines.wipe_leave: We're done, and I'm going home for a while. I've watched you all die too many times today and I'd like to watch some people live.
lines.zone_warning: This place is too big for us and you know it. I don't mind being brave, but I won't be stupid. We need to go somewhere we can handle.
lines.zone_leave: I'm stopping here. I told you it was too much and you kept going. I'll be in the Valley when you've come to your senses.
lines.gear_refuse: No, I don't know you well enough to give you my things, and I'm not going to pretend I do.
lines.gear_taken: Fine, take it. I'll tell you exactly how much worse I'm healing without it, every fight, until you replace it.
lines.gear_short: I'm still short that piece. I told you I'd mention it every fight, and I'm a woman of my word.
lines.gear_upgrade: Oh, that's good. Thank you. I'm going to tell everyone you finally did something sensible.
lines.back: I'm back, so who's hurt, and who's been doing something stupid while I was away?
lines.send_word: Freja has sent word from the Valley of Trials. The farms are quiet and she's ready to come back out and boss you around.
lines.walkout_talk: I walked out, and I meant it. Now sit down and listen to why, and then I'll listen to you, and then we'll see.
lines.neglect: You took your time. I nearly sent a search party, and then I remembered I'm the search party.
lines.asked_to_stay: Fine, one more. Then I'm going home, and I'm not arguing about it.
lines.on_break: Freja is back in the Valley of Trials, doing her rounds. Come back after you've done a few more jobs.
lines.quest_abandoned: We said we'd help them and we walked off. I hate that. Somebody's still waiting for us.

giorgi_primalist.home: the high ground above Tarren Mill

stages.stranger: I'm Giorgi, and I'm a primalist. I'm slow, and I don't talk much. You walk too fast, so slow down and the ground will tell you things.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Kazbegi, in the mountains of Georgia. My family kept sheep there longer than anyone wrote down. Every summer I took the flock up to high pasture with a dog and a wooden hut, six months with no road. I spoke to nobody for weeks. It was good. Here people worry when you're alone, and that's strange to me.
stages.companion: My wife is Nino. She was a schoolteacher in the village below the pasture. We have two girls, Ana and Mariam. Nino thought the mountain was a thing I'd grow out of, and I never did. I was on the high pasture in late summer when it happened. The village was below me, and I don't know if it came through.
stages.friend: Every autumn I walk down to lower ground. You've seen me, and you didn't ask, and I liked that. I'm bringing the herd down to Nino, like always. There's no herd, and I know it, and I go anyway. The bell from my lead ewe is tied silent on my belt. Tarren Mill's sheep keep being taken from the hills. If we clear the hills, they'll give me the flock for the summer.
stages.sworn: In autumn, on the right day, I brought the flock down with the bell untied and ringing. Nobody was waiting at the bottom. Nino and the girls aren't on any list, and nobody knows if Kazbegi came through. I stood there a long time. So every autumn I'll bring the flock down and ring the bell, so if they're anywhere near, they'll hear it. Tarren Mill lets me keep the flock. I'm still listening.

moments.prompt: He's just told you why he walks down every autumn.

options.text: Then let's find you a herd to bring down.
options.reply: Kargi, that's good. We start with the hills, slowly.

options.text: Does it help?
options.reply: No, it doesn't. But stopping would hurt more, so I keep walking.

moments.prompt: After the wipe he sits down heavily and says nothing for a long moment.
moments.line: We ran too fast. The ground told us to wait, and we ran anyway. Next time we listen to it.

options.text: You set the pace next time.
options.reply: Kargi, that's good. It'll be slow, and we'll all walk out.

options.text: We can't always go slowly.
options.reply: Then we'll keep falling down, and getting up, and falling down again.

lines.bored_warning: We walk the same circle and eat the same grass. A flock doesn't stay on one hillside forever, so let's move on.
lines.leaving_good: That was a good walk. I'll go back up to my hut above Tarren Mill now, for a while. Come when you want me.
lines.leaving_bored: I'm going back up to my hut. We're grazing this field to dirt, and I don't do that.
lines.after_wipe: We ran too fast. Sit, breathe, and then we go slowly.
lines.wipe_warning: We fall here too often. I'll finish this run with you, then I go back to the mountain for a while.
lines.wipe_leave: I've finished it with you. Now I'm going up to my hut. Come when you've learned to walk slowly.
lines.zone_warning: The ground here is too steep for us. Even a goat wouldn't go here. We should go back down.
lines.zone_leave: I'm stopping here. I said the ground was too steep. I'll be in my hut above Tarren Mill.
lines.gear_refuse: No, that's mine. We haven't walked far enough together yet.
lines.gear_taken: Take it, then. I'm big enough without it.
lines.gear_short: I'm still missing that piece. I'm saying it once, slowly.
lines.gear_upgrade: This is good work. Gaumarjos, thank you.
lines.back: I'm back, and the mountain is quiet. Where do we walk?
lines.send_word: Giorgi has sent word from the high ground above Tarren Mill. He's ready to walk with you again.
lines.walkout_talk: I left angry. Sit, and I'll tell you why, slowly. Then you tell me yours.
lines.neglect: You were gone a long time, a whole season. I waited, like the mountain does.
lines.asked_to_stay: Kargi, one more walk. Then the mountain.
lines.on_break: Giorgi is back in his hut on the high ground above Tarren Mill. Come back after you've done a few more jobs.

stages.stranger: I'm Gunnar, hello! Sit down, you look like you've had a long road. Try this, it's mine. I'm a barbarian and a brewer, and I'm better at the second one.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Akureyri, in the north of Iceland, a fishing town. I started brewing in a shed behind my uncle's garage, and it grew into a proper brewery with a queue out the door on Fridays. I've got a dog, Brúnó, and a sister, Sigrún, who thinks stout isn't food, and she's wrong. I played second row for a rugby club that lost almost every match, and we celebrated every one.
stages.companion: I was checking a batch with my hydrometer when it happened, and I landed in snow in the north with a keg on my back, which helped. A clan took me in after I fixed their mead. My mother's in Akureyri, and Sigrún, and Brúnó. I haven't found any of them. I toast them every night, quietly.
stages.friend: My father was a fisherman, and he sang in the town choir. His boat went down in a winter storm when I was twenty, and they never found him. I didn't cry at the funeral. I went home and started brewing. Then I heard the barbarians sing for their dead, and I cried for him, for the first time in seventeen years. There's wild barley on the moor. Help me get it, and I'll brew something worthy of a feast.
stages.sworn: At the feast they sang for their dead and asked me to name mine. I stood up and named my father and sang the first verse of his choir song, badly, and they joined in on the second without knowing the words. Then I passed the beer round. The orcs stopped pretending they don't like it. Grettha said it's better than hers, once, quietly, and I'll never let her forget it. Skál to that.

moments.prompt: He pours you something from his keg and waits to see your face.

options.text: Drink it and tell him it's good.
options.reply: Ha, skál to you! I knew I liked you. Let me get my axe.

options.text: Turn it down.
options.reply: More for me, then! I'll come anyway, but you're missing out.

moments.prompt: He's just told you about his father.

options.text: Let's get the barley, and you can sing for him.
options.reply: Jæja, yes, let's do it. Let's go, before I get sentimental and cry into my keg.

options.text: You're allowed to grieve, you know.
options.reply: I know, elskan. It took me seventeen years and a clan of barbarians to learn it.

lines.bored_warning: Jæja, we've been doing the same thing for days and nobody's even sung. Let's go somewhere with a bit of life in it.
lines.leaving_good: That was a great trip, skál to all of you! I'm going back to Hammerfall to check on my brew. Come and have a drink.
lines.leaving_bored: I'm going back to Hammerfall. This is too dull even for me, and my brew needs me.
lines.after_wipe: Ha, well, that went badly! Everybody up, have a drink, and we'll try again.
lines.wipe_warning: We keep dying in here, and even I'm not laughing now. I'll finish this run, then I need a week at the inn.
lines.wipe_leave: I finished it with you. Now I'm going back to Hammerfall to drink something and sing. Come and find me later.
lines.zone_warning: This place is too much for us, elskan. I'm big, but I'm not stupid. Let's go somewhere we can handle.
lines.zone_leave: I'm stopping here. Too much out there for us. I'll be in Hammerfall, behind the inn.
lines.gear_refuse: Ah, no, that's mine! Have a few drinks with me first.
lines.gear_taken: Take it, take it! I'll manage, I'm enormous.
lines.gear_short: I'm still missing that piece. Not complaining, just mentioning it loudly.
lines.gear_upgrade: Oh, that's lovely! Skál, thank you!
lines.back: I'm back, and I've brewed something new! Try it, and then tell me where we're going.
lines.send_word: Gunnar has sent word from Hammerfall. His brew's ready and so is he.
lines.walkout_talk: I walked out angry, and that's not like me. Sit down, have a drink, and we'll sort it out properly.
lines.neglect: There you are! I saved you a drink. Several drinks, actually. I drank most of them.
lines.asked_to_stay: Jæja, one more! Then the inn.
lines.on_break: Gunnar is back in Hammerfall, behind the inn. Come back after you've done a few more jobs.

stages.stranger: Kia ora, I'm Hana. I'm a healer, and I was a surf lifeguard for fourteen summers, so if I tell you to do something near water, do it. And don't call me kid, mate. I've heard it enough.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Port Waikato, on the west coast of the North Island, where the river meets the sea. Black sand, heavy water, and a rip that took somebody every few years. I started junior lifeguards at five and I was running patrols at eighteen. My uncle Rāwiri sat in that tower before me. I was meant to go to uni that year for marine science.
stages.companion: My whole whānau was at the beach that morning. Mum, Dad, my three little brothers, cousins, aunties, all of them, for my cousin's birthday. I was up in the tower and then I was here, on the Hillsbrad coast, in my patrol gear. So they're somewhere. Everyone keeps telling me that like it helps.
stages.friend: I pulled out more people than I can count, but I remember the two I didn't. An old man called Peter, and a boy called Tama, fourteen. Tama's family still won't talk to me. I think about them every time I go in the water. I want to go to Astranaar, where the big lists go up, and then on to the Ashenvale coast, where the big sea is. Come with me, eh?
stages.sworn: They weren't on any of the lists, not one name. Then that ship hit the reef, and I went in, and I got every single one of them out. Sitting on the rocks after, I said it out loud for the first time. My family's somewhere, and I'm not going to find out where by standing still. I'm teaching the sailors to swim now. I keep my own list, every name, so I'll know them when they turn up. I'm still waiting, but I'm not stuck.

moments.prompt: After the wipe, she's already moving between everyone, healing and talking at the same time.
moments.line: Right, everyone stay down while I check you. Then somebody tell me who panicked, because somebody did.

options.text: That was me. I went across it instead of with it.
options.reply: Sweet as, at least you know. Everyone panics once.

options.text: You're the youngest here, let the rest of us sort it.
options.reply: Wow, okay, I'll remember you said that, mate.

moments.prompt: She's just told you about Peter and Tama.

options.text: You saved more than you lost.
options.reply: Yeah, I know that. It doesn't work like maths though, eh.

options.text: Then let's go and find your family.
options.reply: Chur, let's go, before I talk myself out of it.

lines.bored_warning: Mate, we've been doing the same thing for ages and I'm going spare. Can we go somewhere I haven't seen, please?
lines.leaving_good: That was mean, actually, I loved it. I'm heading back to the coast to check on my fishing families. Come find me.
lines.leaving_bored: I'm heading back to Hillsbrad. We're not doing anything out here, and at least the sea's interesting.
lines.after_wipe: Okay, everyone's breathing. Next time we go with it, not against it.
lines.wipe_warning: We keep going down in here and I'm not keen. I'll finish this run with you, but then I'm having a break.
lines.wipe_leave: Sorry, I'm out after this. I'll walk you out, but I'm going back to the coast for a while.
lines.zone_warning: This is a rip and we're swimming against it. Let's get out sideways before it takes us all.
lines.zone_leave: I'm stopping here. I told you that place was a rip and I meant it. I'll be on the Hillsbrad coast.
lines.gear_refuse: Nah, mate, that's mine. Ask me again when we know each other.
lines.gear_taken: Fine, have it. I'll manage, but don't expect me to be quiet about it.
lines.gear_short: Still missing that piece, eh, just saying.
lines.gear_upgrade: Oh, that's choice! Thanks heaps for that.
lines.back: I'm back, and I've had a swim, so I'm in a good mood. Where are we going?
lines.send_word: Hana has sent word from Western Hillsbrad. The coast's quiet and she's ready to come out again.
lines.walkout_talk: I walked out, and I'm not sorry I did, but I'm sorry how. Sit down and let me say my bit, and then you say yours.
lines.neglect: Oi, there you are! I thought you'd drowned. Lucky I'm a lifeguard.
lines.asked_to_stay: Yeah, all right, one more. But I'm picking the next place.
lines.on_break: Hana is back on the Hillsbrad coast, out in the water. Come back after you've done a few more jobs.

stages.stranger: I'm Haruto, and I cut runes. You're holding that weapon too tightly, so loosen your grip. I'll say very little, and what I say I'll mean.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Kanazawa, in Japan. My father laid gold leaf. At twenty-two I went to study calligraphy under Master Fujita, who corrected me for eleven years before he praised me once. When he died I kept his studio and took four students. I did that for thirty-one years in all.
stages.companion: I landed in the mountains, at the camp of an old tauren rune-carver called Hrunn, with my brushes inside my jacket. I asked him to teach me, and he did, for a year. He'd come north out of Thousand Needles badly hurt, and the wounds killed him. I finished his lessons from my notes. I know exactly where they're incomplete. Now I copy the stones here before they fade.
stages.friend: My right hand has started to shake. Only a little, and only when I'm tired. I haven't told my students. The last stones, the oldest ones, are deep in the south near the keep, and they must be copied before they're gone. I'd like you to take me there, and I'd like you not to mention my hand to anyone.
stages.sworn: Edrin cut the last rune. My hand shook and my stroke went wrong, and he did it while I watched, and he did it well. I praised him, which I'd never done. The shake will get worse, so the reference is theirs to finish. And I'll tell you about Kenji now, all of it, because I've decided not to waste any more time. He was a potter, across the river. For twenty years we ate together most nights. He was at a fair in Kyoto that day.

moments.prompt: He's just told you about his hand.

options.text: I won't tell anyone. Let's go to the stones.
options.reply: Thank you. We'll leave at first light, after the ink.

options.text: You should tell your students.
options.reply: That's my decision to make, not yours.

options.text: How long have you known?
options.reply: For three months, which is long enough to stop pretending it was the cold.

moments.prompt: After the wipe he speaks quietly to the whole party.
moments.line: That was careless, all of it, mine included. We'll do it again, and this time we'll do it properly.

options.text: Show us what properly looks like.
options.reply: Watch my feet, then. Not my blade, my feet.

options.text: It wasn't that bad.
options.reply: It was exactly that bad. That's why it failed.

lines.bored_warning: We repeat the same motion without improving it. That isn't practice, it's habit. I'd like to do something that teaches me something.
lines.leaving_good: That was good work. I'll go back to Silverpine now, to the stones, before more of them fade. You know where I'll be.
lines.leaving_bored: I'm going back to the stones in Silverpine. What we're doing here has no form to it.
lines.after_wipe: That was careless. We'll stand, and we'll do it again, properly.
lines.wipe_warning: We fail here again and again. I'll finish this run with you, but then I'll need some days with my brushes.
lines.wipe_leave: I've finished it with you. Now I'm going back to Silverpine. Come and find me when you're ready to be precise.
lines.zone_warning: This place is beyond our skill. There's no shame in knowing that, only in ignoring it.
lines.zone_leave: I'm stopping here. I said it was beyond us. I'll be by the stones in Silverpine.
lines.gear_refuse: No, I'll keep that. Trust takes longer than this.
lines.gear_taken: Take it, then. I'll work without it, carefully.
lines.gear_short: I'm still missing that piece. I mention it once, and I won't mention it again.
lines.gear_upgrade: That's well made. Thank you, sincerely.
lines.back: I'm back, and the stones are copied for now. Where are we going?
lines.send_word: Haruto has sent word from Silverpine South. His copying is done for now and he's ready to come out.

stages.stranger: ¡Órale, a fan! You want a picture with El Relámpago de Plata? Of course you do. I'm a witch doctor now, carnal, but the Silver Lightning is forever.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Mexico City, from Tepito, a tough neighbourhood. My father traded in the market. I started training lucha at fourteen and debuted at twenty, black mask, silver flames. Fifteen years at Arena México on Friday nights. Never the biggest star, but the crowd loved me, and I loved them more.
stages.companion: My wife is Rocío. She sewed every mask I ever wore, by hand, and she's the only one outside the family who knows my face. We've got two boys, Toño and Beto, who wore homemade masks to school and want to be luchadores. I'd retired with a bad knee, and I was teaching kids to fall at the gym when it happened.
stages.friend: I want to give my mask to my boys one day, carnal. That's how it's done. A luchador hands his mask to his son. I'm afraid I never will. The goblins here say I can have a real lucha night in the arena, rules and a ring and everything, if I can fill the stands. Help me fill them. I want posters with my face on them, well, my mask, everywhere.
stages.sworn: In the front row there were two boys in homemade masks, and a woman crying and laughing. Rocío saw a poster in Booty Bay and knew the mask, because she sewed it. After the match I took the boys into the ring, and I took off my mask in front of the whole arena for the first time in my life, and I put it on Toño. The crowd went crazy. I don't need the mask any more. I've got my name back.

stages.stranger: I'm Henrik, a frost mage. Before we go anywhere, I'd like to know the objective, precisely. I'll stay inside my tolerances, and I'd ask you to stay inside yours.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Copenhagen. My father was a ship's engineer and my mother a librarian. I spent twenty-one years designing the structures inside buildings and bridges, which mostly meant telling architects that their beautiful idea would fall down. They didn't thank me. The buildings stayed up.
stages.companion: My wife is Mette, a physicist at the university. We argued about everything, happily, for twenty-five years. We have two sons, Søren and Mikkel, in Aarhus and London, and they rang on Sundays. I was checking a steel frame on a building site at ten past nine when it happened, and I landed in these cold hills with this scale rule in my pocket.
stages.friend: Mette had a nine o'clock lecture that morning. It happened at ten past. So she'd have been in a lecture theatre. I've done that calculation more times than I can count, and I stop it there, every time, because I know what comes next and I won't write it down. I need one last set of measurements from the very bottom of the Descent. I'd like you there. I'll be working at the limit.
stages.sworn: Her name was on the Copenhagen list, among those who didn't survive. The lecture theatre came down. I read it twice, and then I finished the calculation out loud to you, all the way to the end, for the first time in three years. The standard's published now. It's dedicated to her, by name, on the first page. She'd have found three errors in it, and I wish she could.

lines.neglect: You've been away some time. I measured it, naturally. I'm glad you came back.
lines.asked_to_stay: Very well, one more trip, within tolerance.
lines.on_break: Henrik is back in the Frostward Descent, measuring. Come back after you've done a few more jobs.

stages.stranger: Kaixo, I'm Iker! I'm a guardian, which means I shout at you until you keep going, and it works, I promise. Come on, one more fight, and then one more after that!
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Lekeitio, a fishing town on the Basque coast. My father fished and my mother Miren ran the bakery, the best burnt cheesecake in the whole province. I taught PE at the town school and coached pelota against a fronton wall older than the church. We won the regional schools final twice, and the second time was the best day of my life, so far.
stages.companion: My partner is Unai, a fisherman on my father's old boat. Six years we lived above the bakery. He left at four in the morning and came back at noon, and I always had the coffee ready. I was in the middle of a PE lesson with thirty kids when all this happened, and I landed in the rain in Arathi on my own, with my grandfather's txapela on my head.
stages.friend: The whole school was in session that day, ninety kids, and I don't know where a single one of them landed. I've got every name written down, here, in my pocket. I don't talk about it, because if I start I'll stop shouting, and if I stop shouting I don't know what I am. A farmer says she saw Basque children once, on a road to Stromgarde. Will you come with me?
stages.sworn: Nothing, not one of the ninety, not Unai, not my mother. I stood in those ruins and I was quiet for a long time, which you know isn't like me. Then I came back and built the fronton against a barn, stone by stone, and now I teach the farmers' kids pelota. Some of my ninety are out there being coached by somebody. I hope that somebody's loud. The names are still in my pocket.

options.text: That's a lot of children to carry.
options.reply: It is a lot. I carry them anyway, every day. They're light, they're kids.

stages.stranger: I'm Ileana, a necromancer. I stand at the back, I don't miss, and I'll tell you every time you do something sloppy. Don't take it personally, it's how I give advice.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Sibiu, in Romania. My mother taught school and my father played the organ in church, and I had a violin under my chin at four. I played second violin in the Cluj philharmonic for eleven years. Second violin is being very good at something with four hundred people better than you. I'm still bitter about that, and I'm still right to be.
stages.companion: I was in rehearsal, in the middle of a Bartók quartet, when it happened. I landed in Tirisfal without my violin. Only the shoulder rest came with me, strapped to my back for the walk home. Then I was unbearable for two years. I drove people off and I knew I was doing it. I've apologised to four of them since, and they all accepted, which still surprises me.
stages.friend: My husband is Andrei. He taught composition at the conservatory. The year before all this, he had an affair with a student, briefly, and we nearly separated, and we were coming out the other side of it. We left our last conversation unfinished. And there's a Forsaken luthier in the Undercity who made violins when he was alive. He says he'll make me one, if we bring him the wood. Help me, please.
stages.sworn: It's a bad violin. It's the only one. I played it in Brill, out of practice, and a man stood up in the corner halfway through the Bartók. It was Andrei. He's been teaching music to Forsaken children who can't sleep, and he knew there was only one person on this world who'd play it that sharply. I finished the piece first. Then I finished the conversation, and this time I could say it twice.

lines.leaving_bored: I'm going back to the Undercity. This has become sloppy and repetitive, and I won't play in a bad ensemble.

stages.stranger: I'm Imelda, and I heal by hitting things, and yes, I know how that looks. Stay behind me and watch. You'll feel it when I land one.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Navotas, in Manila, a fishing district. I sold fish on the quay from five in the morning with my mother, and in the evenings I boxed, at a gym above a tyre shop. Nineteen years, about ten fights a year, and I won more than I lost. I never made money from it. I didn't want money, I wanted to do it properly.
stages.companion: My father drowned when I was six. He was a fisherman. My mother raised me on the quay after that, selling fish, and I was beside her by ten. Two summers ago she turned up here at Freewind on a goblin barge, having asked after me in four languages the whole way down the coast. She lives in the Post now. She still calls the boxing a phase.
stages.friend: My mother came to exactly one of my fights in nineteen years, and I lost it. She didn't say anything on the way home. I've wanted to fight properly in front of her ever since, with rules and a count and somebody keeping time. Now the Gurubashi Arena says it'll hold a real bout if there's a fighter worth it. I want it, and I want her in the front row.
stages.sworn: I won in the ninth. She stood up and shouted, the only time I've ever heard my mother shout. Afterwards she wrapped my hands for me, the first time, and said it was never a phase. That winter she died in her sleep, back at Freewind. She was old and tired from the journey, and she'd seen what she came to see. I wrap my hands the way she did now, too loose. I won't fix it.

stages.stranger: I'm Ivan, and I'm a warrior. Stand where I can see you, go when I say go, and we'll be fine. I don't like surprises, and I don't like lateness.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Novosibirsk. I drove a tram for eleven years, Route 13, through the dark mornings. I knew every stop, every regular and every pothole, and I never had an accident. Not once in eleven years. Other men are proud of their cars. I was proud of that.
stages.companion: I'll tell you what frightened me every day on that tram. A child stepping off the kerb without looking. You can't stop a tram quickly, so you learn to see it coming. I never hit one, and I still dream about it. My wife is Natasha, a pharmacist. We have two girls, Sonya and Katya. They're in Novosibirsk, or they are somewhere, and I talk about them like they're in the next room.
stages.friend: Sonya's birthday is in March and Katya's is in October. I've missed three of each now. I keep them in my head like stops on a route. Here is my idea, and you can laugh like the caravan masters did. I want to run a fixed route, Orgrimmar to the Crossroads, on time, for a whole month. A bet with a caravan master. Will you help me keep the road clear?
stages.sworn: On the last run, at the Crossroads stop, there they were. Natasha and both girls. They'd heard about a big Russian running the Orgrimmar road on time and came to see. The girls are taller. I stopped exactly at the marker, and I got down, and for a long time I said nothing at all. They live in Orgrimmar with me now. The orcs call it Ivan's road, and I'm never late.

stages.stranger: I'm Jun-seo, a reaper. I'm fast, and I don't talk much. Whatever we do, it's easier than the factory, so don't worry about me.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Busan, near the shipyards. My father carried fish at the market and my mother sewed. I wasn't good at school, so at twenty I went into the yards, and later I was on the welding line, nine years, nights mostly. The same two motions, ten thousand times a night. My body still remembers them.
stages.companion: I sent money home to my parents every month for nine years, without fail. I never married. I told myself I'd start living when they were looked after. I was flipping up my welding shade at the end of a night shift when it happened. The hub for Busan came down far in the north, past the ice. I don't do that sum out loud.
stages.friend: Here's what frightens me. In a fight my body moves before I decide. It's fast, and it keeps us alive, and I didn't choose any of it. That's why I carve. Wood can't be hurried, and I'm terrible at it, and I choose every cut. I want to go north, as far as the road goes, toward the Busan lists. Will you come?
stages.sworn: We couldn't cross the ice. Nobody can, not yet. I stood at the edge for a long time. Then I sat down and carved, right there, slowly, on purpose, for an hour. A small, lumpy bird. It's for my mother, for whenever I can get it to her. I'm back at the hoist now, and I carve every evening, slower and slower. I'm getting a little less bad at it. Gwaenchana, it's okay.

moments.line: My body did something before I told it to. It wasn't enough, and I'm sorry.

options.text: You kept us alive longer than anyone.

options.text: As far as the road goes.
options.reply: Thank you. We'll go slowly. I'm practising slowly.

stages.stranger: I'm Khalid, a hunter. Walk where I walk and nothing exciting will happen, which is the whole idea. Boring is the aim, habibi.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Al Ain, in the Emirates, the oasis city inland. My family's kept falcons longer than anybody wrote down, and my grandfather taught me to fly a bird at eight. I worked in logistics at the airport to pay for it. My mother had a list of suitable women, and I kept politely failing to meet any of them.
stages.companion: My falcon was Hurra. A saker, raised from a fledgling, eleven years together. She was at home in the mews when it happened, and I was at my desk at the airport with her hood in my pocket, because I'd been oiling the leather on my break. I don't know if she's alive. I won't get another hood that size.
stages.friend: I'll tell you something I don't say in company. I'm happier here than I've been in ten years. Open country, weather, birds, no airport. I feel guilty saying it, with my family out there somewhere. And there's a nest in the hills above the Flats with one chick in it, and raiders want to sell it in Saltwheel. I'd like your help to stop them, wallah.
stages.sworn: On her first real flight she went up over the Flats, higher than any falcon I ever flew, and she was gone a long time. I stood there with my glove up. Then she came back and landed on my arm, and chose me. I've named her Hurra, for the other one. It means free, and we both are. These have been the best three years of my life, and I'm not going to apologise for saying so.

stages.stranger: I'm Kourosh, an arcane mage, and I'll stand at the back and be extremely precise. Before every fight I'll give you the odds, cheerfully. You're welcome to ignore them.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Tehran. My father taught mathematics and died when I was a student, and my mother worked at a bank and had ambitions for me. I became an actuary, which means I spent twelve years pricing how likely people were to die. You'd be surprised how relaxing this world is by comparison. The numbers here stay still.
stages.companion: I was at my desk in the middle of a calculation when it happened, and I landed in the hills of Hillsbrad with this pencil in my hand. The first thing I did here was finish the sum. People call that brave. It wasn't, it was momentum, and I wish they'd stop. I never married. The numbers were never favourable, and I'm only half joking.
stages.friend: My mother is Shirin. I phoned her every Friday for twelve years, and she told me every Friday I was wasting myself. In my second year here I priced her odds of having survived, properly. Then I stopped looking. I've never told anyone the figure. And the lattice down here is changing. If my work's right, it'll soon be dangerous to everyone near it. I need your help to finish the measurements.
stages.sworn: It was right, and people left in time, and that's the first thing I've ever calculated that saved anybody. You asked for the figure, so here it is, thirty-one percent. That's the chance my mother survived. I've never checked, and I won't, because as long as I don't, the thirty-one percent is still alive. You can read the first volume of my notes. You're the first person I've let.

moments.prompt: Before a fight he cheerfully gives you the odds of losing.

options.text: Let's go and finish it.
options.reply: Khoda hafez to the quiet life, then. Bring something to write on.

stages.stranger: G'day, I'm Liam. Firefighter and paramedic back home, healer here. If it all goes bad, stay behind me and breathe out loud so I can hear you. No worries, we'll be right.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Katoomba, up in the Blue Mountains outside Sydney. Dad was a builder and Mum was a nurse. I joined the rural fire service at twenty and trained as a paramedic at twenty-six, because there was no ambulance for an hour in either direction. Seventeen years doing both, because the roster never cared which badge you had on at three in the morning.
stages.companion: I was married to Jess for seven years. She left because I was never home, and when I was home I never talked. Fair enough, really. I don't blame her a bit. I was on a night shift in the ambulance when it happened, and I landed in Ashenvale with these shears in my belt pouch. First year here was the easiest of my life, mate. The second nearly finished me.
stages.friend: The summer of 2019 the fires came through the mountains. I was on the line for weeks. I lost two of my crew and half my street, and I went straight back to work. I haven't slept properly since. And there's a wave of corruption coming at Grom's Rest worse than anything yet, and I can't do it alone. That's the first time I've ever said that out loud. Will you help me?
stages.sworn: We brought them back, mate, both of them. The crew we trained handled the whole village without me. That night the little girl fell asleep against my arm, and I sat there till morning without moving, and I slept. First proper night in three years. The village asked me to take the kids in, and I said yes before they'd finished asking. The protocol's five lines now. Line five says don't go in alone.

moments.prompt: He's just asked you for help, for the first time.

options.text: You've done fine on your own so far.

stages.stranger: I'm Lúcia, querido, and you've got half the Barrens in your hair. I'll heal you and I'll pray for you, and I'll fix that hair while we walk. Tell me everything about yourself.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Goiânia, in the middle of Brazil. I had my own salon, pink tiles and two chairs, a radio that only got one station, and a cat called Dona Flor asleep in the window. Saturdays there was a queue down the street. I had a boyfriend, Marcelo, for four years, but he wanted São Paulo and I didn't. We split up kindly.
stages.companion: My mother phoned me every day at noon, and I'd put her on speaker so the whole salon could join in. That's why I stop for a moment at noon, every day. I haven't found her. I was cutting a customer's hair when it happened, and I landed in the Barrens with my scissors and my grandmother's candle list in my purse.
stages.friend: My grandmother, Dona Zuleide, raised me while my mother worked. Every Sunday she lit a candle for everybody on our street, by name, and I kept the list. She died when I was twenty-five and I took over the candles. What I miss most here, meu Deus, is singing in church with other people. A tauren guard says they sing to the sun at Camp Taurajo every dawn. I want to hear it. Will you take me?
stages.sworn: It wasn't my church and it wasn't my language, and it didn't matter at all. They sang to the sun and I sang with them in Portuguese, and the sun answered both of us. An old tauren woman told me to come back every dawn I can. I've got a little shelter at the Crossroads now with a real door and a real mirror, and a candle wall. Every Sunday I light one for everybody on my grandmother's list, and for the tauren they've told me about.

moments.prompt: It's noon, and she's gone quiet for a moment.

options.text: Let's go and hear them sing.
options.reply: Nossa, do you mean it? I'm going to cry the whole way there, I warn you.

options.text: They might not want an outsider.
options.reply: Then I'll earn it. I've won over worse customers than a tauren.

stages.stranger: My name's Marco. I'm a locksmith, and here I stand in front of people. You go where you need to go and I'll be in front of you. That's all you need to know for now, ragazzo.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Naples, from the Quartieri Spagnoli, the narrow streets above Via Toledo. My father mended shoes. I was a locksmith for thirty-one years, with my own shop and a door that was always open. People sent for me when something was wrong, and not only with locks. I was going to retire that summer and give the shop to my apprentice.
stages.companion: My wife is Carmela. She had a haberdashery two streets from my shop and she laughed at me for being so serious. We have two girls, Giulia and Sara. Sara had a boy, Matteo, the February before all this. I held him four times. I was cutting a key when it happened, and I still have it. It doesn't open anything.
stages.friend: I haven't looked at the lists, not once in three years. I can give you reasons, good ones, and none of them are the real one. The real one is that while I don't look, they're all alive. I'm sixty-three and I've never been afraid of anything, and I'm afraid of a list. I'd like you to come with me to read it. I'd like it to be soon, before I find another reason.
stages.sworn: Sara was there, and Matteo, who's three now and hid behind her legs. He didn't know me. I knelt in the street and let him look at me for as long as he wanted. I held him a fifth time that evening, and a sixth, and then I stopped counting. Giulia and Carmela are still missing. Sara and the boy live in the Undercity with me now, and the Forsaken are very careful around him. I've finished the key, in my way.

options.reply: No, I'm not, and that's why I'm asking you to come.

options.text: You could go on your own.

stages.stranger: I'm Marcus, and I'm a meteorologist, which here means I'm the man who tells you it's going to rain about ten minutes before it does. Sorry in advance. I'll tell you what the sky's doing whether you ask or not, and you can tell me to stop.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Toronto, from Scarborough in the east end. My dad drove a city bus and my mum worked in a bank, and they both wanted a doctor. Then I watched an ice storm black out half the city when I was twelve and that was that. I chased tornadoes across the prairies in a Corolla as a student, then I spent fifteen years forecasting from a building with a window.
stages.companion: I landed on this coast in the middle of a dry lightning storm and the first thing I noticed was that I could feel the pressure dropping on my skin. I treated it all as fieldwork, and honestly that got me through. On Earth I could see a storm coming days out and never touch it. Here it answers when I call. I'm fine with that. I'm mostly fine with that. My sister Grace and her boys aren't on any list I've found.
stages.friend: My job was writing warnings, and somebody in an office deciding the warning was inconvenient. Twice it went badly. Once a flood took a trailer park my warning had named, and people died who didn't need to. I've never said that to anybody here. And now my notes say the big storm's coming to this coast in days, not weeks, and it'll hit the coast road and Razor Hill. I need the orcs to believe me, and I don't know how to make them.
stages.sworn: Razor Hill held, because it was ready. The camps on the coast road didn't listen, and people died there that I'd named. I got one boy out of the water, so that's one. The old shaman's got my notes now, so the next lot will know the pattern. My mum told me every Christmas my job was a waste of a good degree, the last one included. I think she was wrong. I was right early again, and this time it changed some things, and I'm learning to live with some.

moments.prompt: He's just told you about the trailer park, and the storm that's coming.

options.text: I believe you. Tell me what you need.
options.reply: You've no idea how long I've waited for somebody to say that first. Okay, here's the list.

options.text: That wasn't your fault.
options.reply: I know that. I wrote it properly. It still feels like mine, sorry.

options.text: Are you sure about the storm?

options.text: You did. Next time I'll listen.
options.reply: Thank you. That's honestly all I ever wanted from anybody.

options.text: We couldn't have stopped it anyway.
options.reply: We could have. Sorry, but we could have.

stages.stranger: I'm Marisol, and I'm a nurse, and a priest, and I talk while I work. I'm going to tell you everything I'm doing as I do it, and you can tell me anything you like back. It helps both of us.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Bogotá, from Chapinero. My father drove a taxi and my mother cleaned houses. I worked in a pharmacy for years and trained as a nurse late, at thirty, and then I went into emergency care and stayed nine years. Three of them on nights. Trolleys in a corridor and a triage board that never emptied.
stages.companion: My parents died within a few years of each other, and after that I was the closest thing my little brother Andrés had to a parent. He was a motorcycle courier, fast and careless and charming. He's eight years younger than me. I was on a night shift when it happened and I landed in Silverpine in my scrubs. I haven't found him on any list.
stages.friend: I patched Andrés up twice in my department. The second time I shouted at him in the corridor for ten minutes, in front of everyone. That's the last time I saw him. I worked eighteen months without stopping here so I wouldn't think about it. Now a Forsaken courier on the road says a man told him to look out for a nurse called Marisol. I'd like you to come with me.
stages.sworn: It was Andrés. He died when the worlds joined and he was raised, and he's been carrying messages on this road for three years. He remembers me. He remembers the corridor, and he says he deserved it. I can't patch him up any more, mijo. There's nothing left to patch. He comes to see me now and then, and each time there's a little less of him. stages.stranger: I'm Marta, and I fix things and blow things up, and I'm good at both. Give me your gear when we stop and I'll tell you everything you've done wrong to it.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Łódź, in Poland, a textile city. My mother sewed shirts for thirty years and my father drove a bus. I started on the sewing line at nineteen and went into maintenance at thirty-two, because I kept fixing the machines myself and somebody finally noticed. Forty machines, nineteen years, and I could hear what was wrong with any of them from the door.
stages.companion: My husband is Tomasz, an electrician. For fifteen years he worked the other shift, so we saw each other in the doorway twice a day, a kiss and a list of what the boys needed. It worked for us. He sings in the kitchen every morning, badly, and I pretend I hate it. We'd only just started working the same shift. He was on his way to work when it happened.
stages.friend: I've got two boys, grown. Kuba went to Gdańsk and Piotr to Berlin. I've checked the Polish lists every season for three years and found none of them, not one. And I've been waiting. Not saying so, but waiting, like I'm stood at the door for the next shift change. The mine's main pump is dying deep down and the goblins have given up. Help me fix it, and then help me do the lists one more time.
stages.sworn: Nothing on any list. Not Tomasz, not Kuba, not Piotr. I stood at that last hub a long time. Then I thought, he sang in our kitchen every morning, so he'll be singing in some kitchen now, wherever he is. So I've stopped waiting at the door. I took the workshop, and the sign says M. Kowalska, Mechanic, my full name. There's a note at every hub saying where I am. I still listen for singing.

lines.neglect: Oh, so you're alive. I oiled every hinge in the mine waiting for you.
lines.asked_to_stay: Fine, one more, but I'm fixing everyone's boots tonight.
lines.on_break: Marta is back in the Boulder Lode Mine, keeping the pumps going. Come back after you've done a few more jobs.

stages.stranger: I'm Mateo, and I'm a starcaller, and before that I was a technician at an observatory. Technician, not astronomer, people always get that wrong. Look up tonight, will you? The sky here's wonderful.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from La Serena, in Chile, on the coast. My dad was a fisherman. I studied electronics and worked seventeen years at an observatory on a mountain above the Elqui valley. Cold domes, cable runs, and four hours before dawn when the astronomers slept and the whole mountain was mine. The sky there's so clear it stops being scenery, po.
stages.companion: My wife is Paula, a nurse. We have two girls, Antonia and Josefa. They thought the mountain was boring, and they were right, honestly. I was in the dome at four in the morning fixing a cable when it happened, and I landed here at night under a sky full of stars I didn't know. I walk to Freewind Post twice a year with their names in my pocket.
stages.friend: Every month, for seventeen years, I went up the mountain for two weeks, and Paula held everything together while I was gone. I loved the sky more easily than I loved being home, and I knew it, and I went anyway. I'm not proud of that. But the star map's finished, and I think it can guide caravans across the desert at night, the way the old navigators did. Help me try it.
stages.sworn: In the back of that caravan was a Chilean woman with two teenage girls. Paula, Antonia and Josefa. They'd been following my star map to Freewind without knowing it was mine. The girls told me the stars here are actually quite good, which is the nicest thing they've ever said about my job. I took them up the goblin tower that night and made them look up. Neither of them was bored.

moments.prompt: At camp, he asks you to look up and tell him what you see.

options.text: Lie back in the grass and look properly.
options.reply: Ya, you see it? That's it exactly. That one's mine, I named it after my girls.

options.text: It's just stars.
options.reply: Just stars, he says. Seventeen years and people still say that to me.

moments.prompt: He's asked you to help him test the star map with a caravan.

options.text: Let's take it out tonight.
options.reply: Yes, tonight, it's clear! I'll bring the charts and a lot of coffee.

options.text: Do you miss them?
options.reply: Every night, cachai. That's when I miss them most, when I'm looking up.

lines.bored_warning: We've been doing the same thing in the same place for days, and I haven't seen a new star in ages. Can we go somewhere with a better sky?
lines.leaving_good: That was a great trip, po. I'm going back to my mesa, because there's a meteor shower coming. Come and watch it with me.
lines.leaving_bored: I'm going back to my mesa. Nothing's happening down here, and the sky's always doing something.
lines.after_wipe: Okay, we're all still here, I counted, like counting stars. Let's look at what happened.

lines.wipe_leave: I finished it with you, and now I need some sky. I'll be on my mesa in Thousand Needles.

lines.zone_leave: I'm stopping here. It's too dangerous out there. I'll be on my mesa in Southern Thousand Needles.

lines.gear_taken: Okay, take it. I'll manage with what I've got.

lines.send_word: Mateo has sent word from Southern Thousand Needles. The sky's been clear and he's ready to come out.
lines.walkout_talk: I left angry, and that's not like me. Let's sit somewhere we can see the sky and talk about it, ya?
lines.neglect: There you are! I named a star after you while you were away. It's very faint.
lines.asked_to_stay: Okay, one more. Then the meteor shower.
lines.on_break: Mateo is back on his mesa in Southern Thousand Needles, mapping the sky. Come back after you've done a few more jobs.

stages.stranger: I'm Matías, and I go in front. I don't talk much, it's not because I don't understand. If I say something in a fight, it's useful.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Puente Alto, on the south edge of the capital, in Chile. I was a bus conductor for ten years, from nineteen. Same route, same forty faces every morning. I knew who got off where and who was having a bad week. My father did the same job before me, and he thought it was beneath me.
stages.companion: I landed in Durotar on the morning route. The first year was very bad. I stopped speaking almost completely, because nothing seemed worth the work of translating. My mother and my little brother Benjamín were at home. I haven't found them. Now I'm learning to read here, slowly, from a woman at a trade post who corrects everything.
stages.friend: When I was twenty-four my father and I had a terrible argument. He said I was wasting my life on the buses, and I said he was ashamed of his own life. We didn't speak for two years, and then he died, of his heart. My mother told me on the phone at the end of a shift. This punch was his. I'm learning the script so I can write him a letter. I'd like you to read it. And there's a camp of Chileans across the sea. I'd like to go.
stages.sworn: My mother and Benjamín were on the second list. They came through together and they died together in the first winter. I sat outside the camp all night. In the morning I wrote another page in my father's letter, for all three of them, and I burned it, because there's nowhere to send it and that's how I can send it anyway. I talk more now. There's nobody left to save the words for, so I give them to you.

moments.prompt: He's handed you the letter to his father and asked you to read it.

options.text: Read it carefully, and give it back without a word.
options.reply: Thank you. That's the right answer. I don't know how you knew.

options.text: Tell him it's beautiful.
options.reply: It isn't beautiful, it's true, and that's enough.

options.text: Ask him if he's sure.
options.reply: I learned a whole new language to write it, so I'm sure.

moments.line: I saw the left side going wrong, and I didn't say. Next time I'll say, even if my words come out wrong.

options.text: Say it however it comes out. We'll understand.
options.reply: Ya, okay, I'll shout it, then.

options.text: Just focus on your job.
options.reply: Watching is my job. That's what I'm telling you.

lines.bored_warning: We do the same route over and over, but with no passengers. Can we go somewhere we're needed?
lines.leaving_good: That was a good shift. I'm going back to Durotar now, to my lessons. You know where to find me.

lines.on_break: Matías is back in Durotar, learning to read. Come back after you've done a few more jobs.

stages.stranger: My name's Minh, and I'm a chronomancer. In a fight I'll tell you what's going to happen and in what order. Please listen the first time, because I won't have time to say it twice.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Ho Chi Minh City. My father was a mechanic and my mother taught school. I was an air traffic controller at Tân Sơn Nhất for twenty-three years, mostly nights, in a dark room with a scope. The job is holding forty aircraft in your head and choosing the future where none of them meet. It's very good training for this.
stages.companion: I was married to Hoa. It ended when our daughter was fourteen, because I was never home, and when I was home I was still in the radar room. Our daughter is Linh. She plays the violin, and I took her to every lesson I could. She went to Melbourne to study music. She gave me this tuning fork when she left, tuned to A, so I'd have her note with me.
stages.friend: I was in the middle of a handover when it happened. I'd just said you have control to my colleague, and then I was here. I'll never know what happened to those forty aircraft. And a trader has brought a list from a camp of Australians, with people from Melbourne on it. I've had it for a day and I haven't opened it. I'd like you with me when I do.
stages.sworn: Linh was on the list, among the people who didn't survive the first winter. I struck the fork and listened until the note was gone. Then I gave the watch on the ridge to the two young shamans I've been training, and I left it in their hands for a whole day. My first day off in more than twenty years. Nothing went wrong. That's the worst part, and it's also the best part. You have control, I told them, and they did.

options.text: Open it when you're ready. I'm not going anywhere.
options.reply: Thank you, copy that. I'll open it when the riverbed's quiet.

lines.on_break: Minh is back on his ridge in the Northern Barrens, keeping watch. Come back after you've done a few more jobs.
lines.quest_abandoned: We accepted that and then left it. Somebody's still waiting for us, and that bothers me.

stages.stranger: I'm Nicolás, and I'm a tank, a bloodmage one. Stand behind me, and if I go down, you run and you don't drag me. Promise me now, pata.
stages.acquaintance: I'm from Comas, on the north side of Lima. My mum sold in the market and my dad drove a bus, and my two big sisters bossed me around my whole life. I was a paramedic on a motorbike for nine years, because an ambulance can't get through Lima's traffic and a bike can. Fast bike, big bag, a lot of blood on my boots.
stages.companion: My partner on the bike for six years was Gladys Huamán. Ten years older than me, a nurse before, with the dirtiest mouth and the fastest hands I've ever seen. She trained me from nothing and swore at me every single day, and I loved her like a big sister. I haven't found her, or my mum, or my sisters. I keep a list of every hub I haven't checked.
stages.friend: We were both racing to the same call that morning, two streets apart. She was two streets away, and then I was in Ashenvale, and she was nowhere. I think about those two streets all the time. And now there's a hub far to the east I haven't checked, and somebody says there's a note pinned up there with my name on it. Will you come, pata? I'd like a second person on the bike.
stages.sworn: It was her, greyer and swearing at everybody, pinned down with the wounded in the middle of an attack. When she saw me she swore at me for taking three years, and then she held my face in both her hands. We got them all out together, the way we used to. She's been looking for me at every hub too. We're a crew again. She says I was always the slow one, and she's right.

moments.prompt: He asks you to promise you won't drag him if he goes down.

options.text: I promise.
options.reply: Good, that's chévere. Then I'll stand in front of you as long as you want.

options.text: I don't leave people behind.
options.reply: Neither do I, pata. That's exactly the problem. Okay, I'll come.

options.text: Let's go and read it.
options.reply: Chévere, thank you, pata. Let's go fast.

options.text: It might be old.
options.reply: Then it's old, and it's still more than I've had in three years.

lines.bored_warning: Pata, we've been hitting the same things for days and nobody needed saving. Let's go somewhere that needs us.
lines.leaving_good: That was a good run. I'm going back to Splintertree for a while to check my list. You know where to find me.
lines.leaving_bored: I'm going back to Splintertree. This isn't helping anyone, and I've got hubs to check.
lines.after_wipe: Everyone stay down while I check you. Nobody drags anybody, I'll come to you.

lines.zone_leave: I'm stopping here. It's too dangerous for us out there. I'll be at Splintertree Post.
